extracted.intended_audience: students, statesmen, and readers of political philosophy studying principles and corruption of governments
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Montesquieu's normative principles about how different regimes should be constituted, how they corrupt, and what institutional features preserve or destroy political virtue. The content is normative political-theory guidance rather than procedural law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of moral/sex laws as instruments of political power
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws punishing immorality (e.g., against women's impudicity) were not aimed solely at moeurs but were used by emperors to punish a crime of impiety or lèse-majesté invented to enforce respect and revenge (examples: Auguste and Tibère).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating such laws, distinguish genuine moral regulation from political instrumentalization: examine whether punishments target moral harm or serve as pretexts to control and punish prominent families. Historians' invectives (Tacitus, Suetonius) indicate the political use of these laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect statutory penalties (no arbitrary increase by rulers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The text notes that the penalty in the law Julia was light, but emperors sought to increase sentences in judgments beyond the law's prescribed punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A lawful system requires adherence to statutory penalties; assess whether magistrates or sovereigns exceed written penalties. If punishments are augmented by executive will, that indicates judicial abuse and tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using ancient legal language to justify new arbitrary crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Tibère's practice: cover newly found crimes with ancient words to cloak new offences (quoting Tacitus: 'Ce fut le propre de Tibère de couvrir de noms anciens des forfaits nouveaux').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to legalistic rhetoric that imports venerable terms (e.g., 'sacrilege', 'lèse-majesté') to legitimize novel coercive measures; this is an anti-pattern of constitutional decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Somptuary laws to restrain luxury (esp. of women)
rubrics_metrics.description: At Rome censors and magistrates enacted particular laws (Fannian, Licinian, Oppian) to maintain women's frugality; debates occurred about revocation (Oppian law controversy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging social-regulation laws, note their connection to public virtue and their political uses; consider whether they target private vice or serve to regulate conspicuous consumption for broader civic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate dowry size by regime type
rubrics_metrics.description: Dots (dowries) should be considerable in monarchies (so husbands can sustain rank/luxury), moderate in republics (where luxury shouldn't reign), and nearly null in despotic states (where women are almost slaves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate marriage-economic rules in light of regime aims: large dowries support aristocratic display; small dowries limit luxury. Use regime context to judge whether dowry rules promote social stability or luxury-driven corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communauté des biens (marital community of property) suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Community of goods between husband and wife is very suitable in monarchies (it involves women in domestic affairs), less suitable in republics (where women have more virtue), and absurd in despotic states (where women are treated as property).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess property regimes against political effects: do they bind women to household duties or enable luxury? Consider cultural/regime fit rather than universal prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules on wives' gains from husbands' property by regime
rubrics_metrics.description: Gains the law grants to women are unnecessary in monarchies, pernicious in republics (produce luxury), and in despotic states should be merely subsistence for survival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing marital property law, weigh the effect of women's independent wealth on public virtue and luxury; tailor rules to avoid incentivizing conspicuous private wealth in republics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meritocratic spouse-selection as civic policy (Samnite custom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Samnite custom: assemble young men, judge them, let the best choose first, next choose second, etc.—rewarding public service, virtue, chastity, beauty, birth, even wealth as 'dot of virtue'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a social institution it promotes virtue and rewards public service without heavy state cost; assess whether social marriage customs can internalize civic virtues in small republics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Women as unsuitable household masters but potentially fit rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: It is against reason that women be masters of the household (weakness makes household dominance illogical), but not that they govern an empire; their weakness gives sweetness and moderation which may produce better government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish micro-level (family) and macro-level (state) roles: evaluate leadership suitability empirically (examples from India, Africa, Muscovy, England) rather than by blanket sex-based prohibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corruption of government begins with corruption of principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The corruption of each government almost always begins with that of its principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In institutional diagnosis, prioritize assessment of underlying principles (spirit, norms) rather than only surface institutions; restoring principles is central to remedying systemic corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: How democracy corrodes: loss and excess of equality
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy is corrupted not only when it loses the spirit of equality, but when it takes equality to an extreme so that everyone wants to be equal to their rulers; the people then usurp magistrates' functions, disrespect senators and elders, and virtue disappears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a democracy, watch for both oligarchic tendencies (inequality) and leveling excesses (everyone wanting to perform government); either extreme signals impending loss of republican virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy's two extremes to avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy must avoid (1) spirit of inequality leading to aristocracy/monarchy and (2) spirit of extreme equality leading to despotism of one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design constitutional checks to guard against both concentration of privilege and mass usurpation of public office; balance delegation and civic deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders corrupt people by flattery and hiding ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who corrupt republics often attach themselves to the people, flatter their grandeur to hide ambition, and flatter their avarice to hide their own greed; this spreads corruption upward and downward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate political rhetoric critically: leaders who incessantly flatter popular appetites often seek to conceal self-interested power grabs—this is an early-warning sign of corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corruption produces vote-buying and small tyrants
rubrics_metrics.description: Corruption increases when the people divide public funds among themselves and combine laziness with management of affairs; suffrages can be bought with money, leading to the rise of small tyrants and eventual loss of liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor public distribution of resources and clientelism; institutionalize accountability to prevent conversion of public benefits into private vote-buying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocracy corrupts when nobles become arbitrary and hereditary
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristocracy is corrupted when nobles' power becomes arbitrary; extreme corruption is hereditary aristocracy (oligarchy), which reduces moderation and civic virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate aristocratic regimes for legal constraints on nobles and for modes of recruitment; hereditary privileges and lack of legal restraint predict oligarchic degeneration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sizing noble class affects power and security
rubrics_metrics.description: If nobles are few, their power is greater but security (sûreté) less; if many, power less but security greater: power grows while safety decreases up to the despotic extreme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how the size/composition of ruling elites affects incentives: institutional design should balance scale of elite power and internal checks to avoid domination or softness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserving aristocratic principle by making command perilous
rubrics_metrics.description: An aristocracy can keep its principle if laws make the perils and fatigues of command outweigh its delights, and if the state has something to fear (internal danger) and uncertainty from outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To sustain elite civic responsibility, create institutional costs/risks to officeholders and maintain external threats or rivalries that preserve martial and public virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarchy corrupts by centralizing prerogatives and micromanaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Monarchies corrode when princes remove prerogatives of corporate bodies or municipal privileges and attempt to govern everything immediately themselves—transforming inspection into direct control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess monarchy for delegation and respect for corporate bodies; centralization of functions is a sign of monarchic decay toward despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarchy corrupts when honors contradict virtue or are debased
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of monarchy is corrupted when first dignities mark servitude, honors can coincide with infamy (e.g., statues and triumphal ornaments given to delators), or when public honors are vulgarized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for politicization or sale of honors, and for instances where honors reward servility rather than merit—this indicates erosions of monarchical legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarchy corrupts when justice becomes severity and menace
rubrics_metrics.description: The monarchy deteriorates when rulers change justice into severity (use of fear and terror, symbolic intimidation like Medusa’s head on breast), promoting servile vanity and frightening imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish firm justice from arbitrary severity; the adoption of threatening symbolism and paranoia-driven punishments signals corruptive slide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Despotism’s intrinsic corruptibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Despotism corrupts continually because of an internal vice: it survives only when external circumstances (climate, religion, situation, genius of the people) force order temporarily without changing its ferocity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat despotism as structurally unstable morally; reforms must address deeper social/cultural constraints that tame despotism rather than rely on its internal transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle determines law effect: good laws become bad if principles corrupt
rubrics_metrics.description: When principles are corrupted, good laws become harmful and turn against the state; conversely, when principles are sound, even bad laws may have the effect of good ones—'la force du principe entraîne tout.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate laws relative to the prevailing civic spirit: legal reform without restoring foundational principles will likely fail or backfire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional checks must fit civic character (Cretan insurrection example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Crete employed a singular check—periodic insurrection by citizens to put magistrates back into private life as a legal mechanism—which succeeded only because of exceptional patriotism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing extraordinary checks, ensure they align with civic character/patriotism; transplanting such institutions to other polities without matching social virtues risks collapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public exercises and institutions' effects depend on civic virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Gymnastics and public games were beneficial when the state had virtue (military training), but when virtue waned they promoted vice and turned young men into mere dancers/baladins rather than warriors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate cultural/institutional practices by their social context: the same institution may strengthen or weaken the polity depending on prevailing moeurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative/procedural changes (who judges) reflect and affect corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Shifts in who sits as judges (senators, equites, tresoriers, centurions) in Rome accompanied and aggravated corruption; moving judicial prerogatives among bodies does not cure corruption if principles are gone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional tinkering about personnel/jurisdiction is insufficient; diagnose whether change addresses principle-level decay before expecting improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: State size determines appropriate regime type
rubrics_metrics.description: A republic naturally suits a small territory (public good better known, abuses less extensive); a mediocre-sized state suits a monarchy; a very large empire implies despotism (centralized, changing law in a single head).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use territorial scale as a key variable in regime design: expect different institutional forms and vulnerabilities depending on a state's size and the distribution of fortunes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation of principles requires maintaining state scale
rubrics_metrics.description: To preserve the principles of an established government one must maintain the state's existing size; enlarging or shrinking alters the spirit of government and leads to principle changes and corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing reforms or expansions, consider the institutional and moral consequences of changing the state's scale; major territorial changes often demand constitutional rethinking.
